Base Threat: Uencrypted data can be intercepted in transit
Model Threat: Connection strings for Azure Cognitive Service, Storage, Application Insights, and Azure Monitor—deployed from GitHub secrets to the IoT Edge device—are stored in plain text on disk or in environment variables readable by other processes on the device. Any process or attacker with access to the device can extract these secrets, gain direct access to Azure resources, read confidential debug frames or telemetry, and impersonate the application from other locations.

Base Threat: Uencrypted data can be intercepted in transit
Model Threat: If WebSocket connections between M1, M2, and M3 on the public-access LAN are not encrypted, an attacker with LAN access can sniff network traffic and reconstruct live video frames, OCR text, and scan results as they traverse the network. Exposure of confidential video content, order information, and potentially personal or sensitive data, leading to privacy violations and regulatory non-compliance.

Base Threat: Uencrypted data can be intercepted in transit
Model Threat: Debug data and feedback frames uploaded by M2 to Azure Storage are stored in a container accessible using a high-privilege connection string; if the storage account or connection string is misconfigured (e.g., overly broad access or exposed in logs), external parties can list and download stored frames. Large-scale leakage of historical video frames and associated data intended only for debugging, exposing long-term records of sensitive operational environments or individuals captured on camera.

Base Threat: Uencrypted data can be intercepted in transit
Model Threat: Telemetry sent to Application Insights and Azure Monitor may include sensitive content (e.g., snippets of OCR results, partial video frame data, or identifiers) and is accessible to a broad set of Azure subscribers or administrators within the tenant without strict role separation. Personnel who do not need access to raw or derived confidential data can view it via monitoring tools, increasing the insider threat surface and violating least-privilege principles for confidential information.

Base Threat: Unauthorized Access to M1 IoTEdge Module
Model Threat: A vulnerability in one of the IoT Edge modules (e.g., M1’s web application) allows remote code execution inside its container, and container or host runtime is misconfigured such that the attacker can access host resources and other module containers. Attacker moves from controlling a single module to controlling the entire IoT Edge device, gaining access to all secrets, video data, and the ability to manipulate interactions with Azure services and IoT Hub.

Base Threat: Unauthorized Access to M1 IoTEdge Module
Model Threat: An attacker who obtains a high-privilege Azure Storage connection string from the Edge device uses it from an external environment to perform administrative operations on the storage account (e.g., create SAS tokens, modify access policies). Attacker escalates from being able to read a subset of debug frames to fully administering the storage account, potentially granting broader access to additional containers or applications and enabling large-scale data exfiltration or tampering.

Base Threat: Dos attack on all IoTEdge Modules since there is no Authentication
Model Threat: An attacker on the local network sends a flood of HTTP requests to M1’s public-access LAN endpoint from multiple machines, exhausting CPU, memory, or network resources on the IoT Edge device. Legitimate users lose access to live video streaming and order scanning functionality; the IoT Edge device may become unstable or unresponsive, disrupting business operations relying on real-time processing.

Base Threat: Dos attack on all IoTEdge Modules since there is no Authentication
Model Threat: A malicious or compromised Browser repeatedly triggers intensive OCR and Text-to-Speech requests via M1/M2/M3 to Azure Cognitive Service, intentionally driving the service beyond its rate or quota limits. Azure Cognitive Service throttles or rejects further requests, halting legitimate OCR and audio processing and potentially degrading service for other applications sharing the same Cognitive Service instance.

Base Threat: Dos attack on all IoTEdge Modules since there is no Authentication
Model Threat: A bug or malicious logic in M2 causes massive uploads of feedback frames to Azure Storage (e.g., an infinite loop writing large blobs), exhausting storage capacity or hitting request-rate limits. Storage operations required for legitimate debugging and possibly other applications are disrupted; added costs and inability to store new diagnostic data hamper troubleshooting and system reliability.

Base Threat: Dos attack on all IoTEdge Modules since there is no Authentication
Model Threat: An attacker who gains partial control over IoT Hub configuration sends frequent, large deployment updates or restarts to the IoT Edge device’s modules (M1, M2, M3, EdgeRuntime), forcing constant restarts. Continuous service flapping on the IoT Edge device prevents processing of video frames and telemetry; the device becomes effectively unusable for its intended IoT workloads.

Base Threat: Application Insights is connected via Connection String which is stored in .env file on the IoTEdge device. Once user gains access to the device, .env file can be read and attacker can tamper the log data.
Model Threat: An attacker with access to the local network or compromised module intercepts and modifies WebSocket traffic between M1, M2, and M3 (if not protected with integrity mechanisms/TLS), altering video frames or order scanning results in transit. Corrupted or manipulated visual and OCR data, leading to incorrect business decisions, mis-processed orders, or fraudulent outcomes based on forged scan results.

Base Threat: Application Insights is connected via Connection String which is stored in .env file on the IoTEdge device. Once user gains access to the device, .env file can be read and attacker can tamper the log data.
Model Threat: An attacker with limited access to the IoT Edge device filesystem (e.g., via another low-privileged process) modifies configuration files or environment variables that contain Azure Storage, Cognitive Service, or Application Insights connection strings. Modules may send data to attacker-controlled Azure resources, leak confidential data, or be prevented from sending data to the legitimate services; attacker also gains ability to act with the privileges of the modified connection strings.

Base Threat: Application Insights is connected via Connection String which is stored in .env file on the IoTEdge device. Once user gains access to the device, .env file can be read and attacker can tamper the log data.
Model Threat: A malicious insider or compromised process alters the debug data or feedback frames that M2 uploads to Azure Storage (e.g., overwriting original frames with forged ones or corrupting stored blobs). Debugging and forensic analyses become unreliable; operations teams may be misled about the root cause of issues or may miss evidence of other attacks, impairing incident response and system reliability.
